summary: In March 2025 the Kubernetes project announced patches in ingress-nginx v1.12.1 and v1.11.5 for a batch of critical vulnerabilities that could make it easy for attackers to take over a cluster. The announcement is short on technical detail, so this file is mostly about response.

overview.background: ingress-nginx is a widely used Kubernetes ingress controller. The announcement says over 40 percent of Kubernetes administrators use it.
systems: Its admission webhook (per the card, not read on the page)
overview.impact: A vulnerable controller could let attackers take over the cluster, according to the blog.
overview.gaps: The blog excerpt read does not give technical details. The card describes the admission controller path; this file treats that as the card's claim.

archNote: Components and relationships come from the cited source where it describes them. Layout and labels are ours.

timeline.e: Vulnerabilities are found and reported in ingress-nginx.
The Kubernetes project publishes patches v1.12.1 and v1.11.5 and a blog post.
Cluster owners learn they run an affected version.
Teams check version, exposure and logs.
Teams upgrade to a fixed version.
Teams confirm the fixed version runs and review for compromise.

rootCause.trigger: A batch of critical vulnerabilities in ingress-nginx.
rootCause.underlying: The blog says they could make it easy for attackers to take over a cluster; details are not in the excerpt read.
contributing: Very wide use of the component

evidence.label: The headline
evidence.body: a batch of critical vulnerabilities that could make it easy for attackers to take over your Kubernetes cluster

evidence.label: A simulated version check
evidence.body: $ kubectl get pods -A -l app.kubernetes.io/name=ingress-nginx -o jsonpath='{..image}' | tr ' ' '\n' | sort -u
evidence.note: Lists controller images so you can see the version. Output omitted.

diagnose.step: Check how the controller is exposed.

correct.step: Restrict network access to the controller.
Rotate secrets if compromise is possible.

fix.safety: Rotating secrets can break workloads. Do it in order with a test plan.

troubleshoot.scenario: You run ingress-nginx in many clusters. A critical advisory arrives.
troubleshoot.question: What is your plan?
hints: How do you check for abuse?
troubleshoot.answer: Inventory versions, upgrade internet-facing clusters first, restrict access, review logs and rotate secrets as needed.

rootcause.q: Which fixed versions did the blog name?

remediation.answer: Query all clusters for controller images.

design.answer: Version inventory, automated upgrades by ring, policies, scanning and alerts.
